suppressed_findings.title: Bare except with unguarded unlink can mask the original error
suppressed_findings.description: If os.replace has already succeeded, or if the failure happened after the temp file was removed, os.unlink(tmp_name) raises FileNotFoundError and hides the original exception. The bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. In that case the cleanup error replaces the real I/O failure, so callers see a misleading error.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): os.unlink(tmp_name)` (or `except Exception`) and then re-raise the original error.

suppressed_findings.title: Expired sessions are no longer removed on access
suppressed_findings.description: The old get() deleted an expired session when it was looked up. The new get() only returns None, so expired entries stay in memory (and in the file for FileSessionStore) until purge_expired is called. If nothing calls purge_expired, the store grows without bound and expired sessions keep being persisted.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Make sure purge_expired runs periodically, or remove the expired entry under the write lock in get().

suppressed_findings.title: Bare except cleanup can mask the original error and leave a temp file
suppressed_findings.description: If the failure happens after the tmp file was already removed or never created, or os.replace succeeded and a later step raised, `os.unlink(tmp_name)` can itself raise FileNotFoundError, masking the real error (e.g. disk full, JSON failure). The bare `except:` also catches KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit. Also, if os.fdopen itself fails, fd leaks.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `try: os.unlink(tmp_name) except FileNotFoundError: pass` around the cleanup, then re-raise; or use contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError).

suppressed_findings.title: Expired sessions no longer removed on get, so they accumulate until purge_expired is called
suppressed_findings.description: The previous get() deleted expired sessions lazily. The new version only returns None, so expired entries (and, in FileSessionStore, their persisted records) grow unbounded unless a caller periodically invokes purge_expired. Existing callers relying on lazy cleanup now leak memory and file size.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Either remove the expired session under the write lock in get(), or ensure purge_expired is scheduled and documented.

suppressed_findings.title: Bare except cleanup can mask the original error and leak the temp file
suppressed_findings.description: If `os.fdopen` fails, `fd` is never closed. If `os.replace` succeeds and the exception is raised later (e.g. KeyboardInterrupt), or the temp file is already gone, `os.unlink(tmp_name)` raises FileNotFoundError and replaces the original exception. A bare `except:` also catches BaseException, which is too broad here.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use `except BaseException:` with `contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError)` around the unlink, or a try/finally that removes the temp file only if it still exists; close the fd if fdopen fails.

suppressed_findings.title: Expired sessions are no longer removed on get, so they accumulate until purge_expired is called
suppressed_findings.description: The old `get` deleted expired sessions on access. The new one only returns None, and nothing else calls `purge_expired`. Expired sessions stay in memory and, in FileSessionStore, are rewritten to disk on every commit, so the store and file grow without bound unless a caller purges regularly.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Either document and schedule `purge_expired`, or purge expired entries inside `create`, which already takes the write lock.

suppressed_findings.title: A corrupt or partially written session file crashes startup
suppressed_findings.description: `_load` only handles FileNotFoundError. Invalid JSON, a missing key or a malformed timestamp raises JSONDecodeError, KeyError or ValueError from the constructor, so the application cannot start until the file is removed by hand.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch decode errors in `_load`, log them, and start with an empty store (or move the bad file aside).

suppressed_findings.title: Missing/inactive product lookups are not negatively cached, and exceptions bypass cache; but inactive stale result returned after deactivate by other writers
suppressed_findings.description: product() caches the full Product row (including inactive ones) under the sku key, which is fine, but a loader that raises UnknownProduct is never cached, so repeated lookups of nonexistent SKUs always hit the repository. This is a degraded-performance edge path (cache-miss amplification for bad SKUs).
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Cache a sentinel for missing SKUs (with TTL) or accept the cost explicitly.

suppressed_findings.title: Writes in the service can race with in-flight loads that were started before the write but invalidate happens after save
suppressed_findings.description: The write path saves to the repository and then invalidates. A reader that loaded the old row before save and stores it after save but before invalidate is protected by the generation check only if invalidate occurs after store. Since invalidate bumps generation after the save, a loader that began after the generation snapshot but read the old row before save will have its store rejected only if the store happens after invalidate; if it stores between save and invalidate, invalidate then removes the key, so this is safe. No defect here.

suppressed_findings.title: remove() now has a check-then-delete race and ignores delete result
suppressed_findings.description: Previously remove() raised UnknownProduct when delete returned False. Now it fetches first and ignores delete's return value; if another writer removes the product between _fetch and delete, the delete silently does nothing and no error is raised, whereas the old code reported it as unknown. Also an extra repository read is added.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Keep the original `if not self._repository.delete(sku): raise UnknownProduct(sku)` and fetch the product only to know the category for invalidation (tolerating a missing row).

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition(":") breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: urlsplit("//[::1]:5000") correctly yields hostname "::1" and port 5000. partition(":") splits at the first colon, so sn_host becomes "[" and sn_port becomes ":1]:5000". The later int(sn_port) then raises ValueError, or the server binds to a bogus host. Any SERVER_NAME with an IPv6 address now breaks app.run().
findings.suggestion: Keep the urlsplit-based parsing, or use rpartition(":") and handle bracketed IPv6 hosts explicitly.

findings.title: Cookie domain computed by splitting host on first colon
findings.description: ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0] returns "[" for an IPv6 host such as "[::1]:5000", and an empty string if the host is empty. The previous code used urlsplit(...).hostname with a "localhost" fallback. The session cookie is now stored under the wrong domain, so session_transaction changes are not sent on later requests. The empty-host case no longer falls back to "localhost".
findings.suggestion: Restore urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost" (urlsplit is still imported in testing.py).

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing with partition(":") breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: `server_name.partition(":")` splits at the first colon. An IPv6 SERVER_NAME such as `[::1]:5000` yields host `[` and port `:1]:5000`. `int(sn_port)` then raises ValueError in `app.run()`. The previous `urlsplit` handled bracketed IPv6 and also stripped any userinfo, so this is a regression.
findings.suggestion: Keep using `urlsplit(f"//{server_name}")` for `hostname` and `port`, or use `rpartition(":")` and handle brackets explicitly.

findings.title: Cookie domain derived by partitioning host on first colon; empty host not handled
findings.description: `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` replaces `urlsplit(host_url).hostname or "localhost"`. For an IPv6 host such as `[::1]:5000`, it yields `[` instead of `::1`, so the cookie is stored against the wrong domain. An empty host now gives "" instead of the "localhost" fallback. The result is that session cookies set by `session_transaction` may not be sent on later requests. The old code also lowercased the hostname, and this does not.
findings.suggestion: Restore `urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost"`.

suppressed_findings.title: urlsplit import still needed but removed usage in session_transaction
suppressed_findings.description: The `urlsplit` import is still used in EnvironBuilder, so this is not a bug. However, the host handling is now duplicated, with `urlsplit` in one place and `partition` in another, and the two can drift apart.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use one consistent host-parsing approach.

findings.title: SERVER_NAME parsing via partition breaks IPv6 literals
findings.description: `server_name.partition(":")` splits on the first colon. For an IPv6 SERVER_NAME such as `[::1]:5000`, host becomes `[` and port becomes `:1]:5000`. Then `int(sn_port)` raises ValueError in `run()`, or the host is wrong. The previous `urlsplit` code handled bracketed IPv6 correctly and also validated the port.
findings.suggestion: Keep using `urlsplit(f"//{server_name}")` to get hostname and port, or parse bracketed hosts explicitly.

findings.title: Cookie domain derived by partition on host breaks IPv6 and drops localhost fallback
findings.description: `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` splits on the first colon. For an IPv6 host like `[::1]:5000`, it yields `[`, so the cookie domain is wrong and session cookies are not matched on later requests. The old code used `urlsplit(...).hostname or "localhost"`, which handled IPv6 and gave a fallback for an empty host. An empty host now yields an empty string.
findings.suggestion: Restore `urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost"`.

findings.title: RootModel.__copy__ shares private attribute state with the original
findings.description: The change removes the step that copied `__pydantic_private__`. For RootModel, the class attribute `__pydantic_private__ = None` shadows the slot, so private attributes live in `self.__dict__['__pydantic_private__']`. `copy(self.__dict__)` is only a shallow copy, so the copy and the original now share the same private dict. Setting a private attribute on one instance, for example `copy.copy(m)._x = 1`, also changes the other. The removed code also dropped `PydanticUndefined` placeholders for unset private attributes. Without that, those placeholders are carried into the copy, so unset privates can appear as sentinel values or leak into the copy.
findings.suggestion: Restore the copy of the private dict in `__copy__`, filtering out `PydanticUndefined` values, so each instance owns its private state.

findings.title: RootModel.__copy__ now shares the private-attributes dict with the original
findings.description: RootModel sets `__pydantic_private__ = None` as a class attribute, so the real private-attributes dict lives in the instance `__dict__`. `__copy__` shallow-copies `__dict__` and only re-copies `root`. The removed block built a new private dict, so the copy no longer aliases the original's. Without it, `copy(model)` and the original share the same `__pydantic_private__` dict. Setting a private attribute on one instance then changes the other. The removed code also dropped `PydanticUndefined` placeholders, so unset private attributes are now carried into the copy.
findings.suggestion: Restore the removed block so the copy gets its own private dict, and keep filtering out `PydanticUndefined` values. For example, `new_dict['__pydantic_private__'] = {k: v for k, v in private.items() if v is not PydanticUndefined}`.

findings.title: Removing the file-position restore leaves the upload at EOF after bytes extraction
findings.description: The deleted `_read_file_bytes` recorded the file position, read the whole file, then seeked back. Now `value.read()` is called directly, so the underlying `UploadFile` stays at EOF. The same `UploadFile` in the parsed form can be consumed again, for example by an `UploadFile` parameter with the same field name in another dependency or body field, or by a second `_extract_form_body` pass over the same form data. That second consumer then reads empty content. The same applies to the list-of-bytes branch at line 1078.
findings.suggestion: Restore the helper that saves the position and seeks back after the read (`position = file.file.tell(); try: return await file.read() finally: await file.seek(position)`), and use it in both places.

findings.title: Removed file position restore makes bytes reads consume the UploadFile
findings.description: The deleted `_read_file_bytes` helper restored the file position after reading. The replacement calls `value.read()` directly and leaves the position at EOF. The parsed form is cached and shared, so the same UploadFile can be read more than once. This happens when several dependencies or the endpoint declare `File()` or `Form()` params for the same field, or when one field is typed as both `bytes` and `UploadFile`. Any later read, including the endpoint's own `await file.read()`, then returns `b''`, which gives empty or truncated content. The same problem applies to the list-of-bytes branch.
findings.suggestion: Keep the helper that saves the position with `tell()`, reads, and then seeks back in a `finally` block. Use it at both call sites.

findings.title: File position no longer restored after reading UploadFile into bytes
findings.description: The removed `_read_file_bytes` helper saved the file position and seeked back after `read()`. Now `value.read()` leaves the underlying file at EOF. The same UploadFile object in the form data can be consumed again, for example when two dependencies or parameters read the same form field, one as `bytes` and one as `UploadFile`. In that case the second consumer reads an empty file. The same happens in the bytes-sequence branch for list fields.
findings.suggestion: Restore the helper (record `file.file.tell()`, read, then `await file.seek(position)` in a `finally`) and use it in both places.

findings.title: Multiple waiters share one Deferred, so later waiters receive None
findings.description: The removed code gave each waiter its own Deferred, chained from the shared one with a callback that returned the result. The new code awaits the shared `parser` Deferred directly. `maybe_deferred_to_future` adds a callback to it, and that callback returns None, or the result is consumed. In Twisted, a Deferred's callback chain passes each callback's return value to the next one. So when several requests to the same netloc wait on one Deferred, the first waiter gets the RobotParser and every later waiter gets None. `process_request_2` returns early on None, so those requests skip the robots.txt check and are allowed through. This is a robots.txt bypass for concurrent requests to a host whose robots.txt is not yet fetched.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-waiter Deferred. Add a callback to the shared Deferred that fires the waiter and returns the result unchanged, then await the waiter.

findings.title: Multiple waiters share one Deferred whose result is not preserved
findings.description: The old code gave each waiter its own Deferred and chained it onto the shared parser Deferred via a callback that returned the result unchanged. The new code awaits the shared Deferred directly. maybe_deferred_to_future adds callbacks to that Deferred, and the callback it adds does not pass the result through. Once the first waiter consumes the result, later waiters (concurrent requests to the same netloc) get None or a stale result, so the parser is treated as missing and robots.txt rules are skipped. If the Deferred has already fired by the time a waiter awaits it, it is also unclear what value it holds. Requests that should be denied may therefore be allowed.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-waiter Deferred, with a callback chained onto the shared one that passes the result through, and await that Deferred. Alternatively, store a future or event that is resolved once and awaited by every waiter.

findings.title: Multiple waiters share one Deferred, so later waiters get a wrong result
findings.description: The change drops the per-waiter Deferred and awaits the shared parser Deferred directly. A Deferred holds a single callback chain. When several requests for the same netloc await it at once, maybe_deferred_to_future adds a callback to the shared Deferred that returns None. The first waiter gets the RobotParser, but the next waiter's callback receives None. Any request after the first therefore sees rp=None, so process_request_2 skips the robots.txt check and the request is allowed even if it is disallowed. A second effect is that the shared Deferred can end up holding a non-parser result for anyone who awaits it later.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-waiter Deferred that is fed from the shared one through a callback that returns the result unchanged, as in the removed code. Alternatively, store an asyncio.Future or an event and give every waiter the same result.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with unparseable ETA
findings.description: The `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` was removed. When ETA conversion raises OverflowError/ValueError, `eta` stays None and execution continues. The request has already been rejected, but it then falls through to `task_reserved(req)`, the callbacks and `handle(req)` (or `limit_task`), so the task is executed immediately even though it was rejected and dropped from the queue. It also leaves the worker's bookkeeping inconsistent, since the message is both rejected and reserved or run, and its ack/reject will be handled twice.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` right after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Task failure no longer recorded in result backend for invalid ETA
findings.description: The `mark_as_failure` call was removed, so a task rejected because of an invalid ETA never gets a FAILURE state in the result backend. Clients waiting on the result will hang or see PENDING forever, because the message is dropped without any record of the failure.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `req.task.backend.mark_as_failure(...)` call before the reject.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with invalid ETA
findings.description: The `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` was removed. When ETA conversion raises OverflowError/ValueError, `eta` stays None and execution falls through. The request has already been rejected, but it is then reserved and passed to `handle(req)` (or rate-limited) and executed immediately. The task runs without its ETA, and the message is acked or rejected twice.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` right after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Failure no longer recorded in result backend for invalid ETA
findings.description: The `mark_as_failure` call was removed. A task rejected because of an unconvertible ETA no longer gets a failure state in the backend, so clients waiting on the result never see the error and may hang or see PENDING.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `req.task.backend.mark_as_failure(...)` call before rejecting, or confirm that dropping it is intended.

findings.title: Missing return after rejecting task with invalid ETA
findings.description: The `return` after `req.reject(requeue=False)` was removed. When the ETA can't be converted, `eta` stays None and execution continues. The task is then rate-limited, reserved, and passed to `handle(req)`, so it runs immediately even though it was already rejected and its message dropped. The task may execute without an ETA and its message is acked or rejected twice.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `return` right after `req.reject(requeue=False)`.

findings.title: Failure no longer recorded in result backend for invalid ETA
findings.description: The `mark_as_failure` call was removed. A task rejected because of an unparseable ETA now leaves no failure state in the result backend, so clients waiting on the result will hang or see PENDING indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Restore the `mark_as_failure` call before rejecting the request.

findings.title: Cached result list is returned by reference and can be mutated by callers
findings.description: find() returns the same list object that is stored in the cache, on both a hit (line 63) and a miss (line 68). Before this change every call built a fresh list. A caller that sorts, appends to or pops from the result now silently corrupts the cached entry, so later callers with the same query get the modified list.
findings.suggestion: Store the list as a tuple, or return list(entry[1]) and list(hits) so callers get a copy.

suppressed_findings.title: Expired entry is popped, so cache may be evicted needlessly
suppressed_findings.description: The lookup pops the key before checking the TTL, so an expired entry has already been removed when the size check runs. That is fine. On an expired miss with a full cache, however, the size check can evict an unrelated live entry even though a slot was just freed by the pop. This wastes cache entries.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Make the eviction check run only when the key is not already present, or run it after accounting for the popped entry.

findings.title: Cached result list is returned by reference and can be mutated by callers
findings.description: find() returns the same list object that is stored in the cache, on both the hit path (line 63) and the miss path (line 68). Before this change each call produced a fresh list. A caller that sorts, appends to or clears the returned list now corrupts the cached entry, and later callers with the same query get the altered results until the TTL expires or a product is added.
findings.suggestion: Store a tuple in the cache and return list(entry[1]) on each call, or return a copy of the list on both paths.

findings.title: Cached result list returned by reference and can be mutated by callers
findings.description: find() returns the same list object that is stored in the cache, on both the hit path (entry[1]) and the miss path (hits). A caller that sorts, appends to or removes from the returned list corrupts the cached value, so later identical queries return the altered results. Before this change each call returned a fresh list.
findings.suggestion: Store a tuple in the cache and return list(...) copies, or return a copy (list(hits)) on both the hit and miss paths.

suppressed_findings.title: Expired entries are popped and refreshed handling is inconsistent with LRU eviction
suppressed_findings.description: The code pops the entry and re-inserts it on a hit to maintain LRU order, but the stored timestamp is unchanged, so the entry is evicted by TTL regardless. That is fine. However, when the entry is stale it is popped and then the capacity check runs against a cache that already lost this key. This is correct, but the eviction at line 66 removes the oldest-inserted key, which is LRU only because hits re-insert. This is subtle but works; the real issue is that the TTL-expired entries of other keys are never purged and linger until evicted.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Optionally purge expired entries when the cache is full, before evicting the LRU entry.

findings.title: Coroutine from deliver() is not awaited
findings.description: deliver is now async, but flush calls it without await. The returned coroutine object is always truthy, so every digest is treated as delivered, and nothing is actually sent. Lines are removed from the queue (data loss), failed is always empty, and Python emits a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

suppressed_findings.title: Queue mutation during await can break iteration and drop entries
suppressed_findings.description: Once deliver is awaited, other tasks may call add() during the await. add() on the defaultdict can insert a new recipient key while flush iterates over sorted(self._pending). Iterating a sorted copy is safe, but self._pending[recipient] on line 42 is fine only if the key still exists. A concurrent flush could also delete the recipient key, so `del self._pending[recipient]` at line 48 could raise KeyError, and a concurrent flush could double-send the same lines.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Guard flush with an asyncio.Lock, or use self._pending.get(recipient) and pop(recipient, None) when removing the entry.

findings.title: deliver() coroutine is not awaited in flush
findings.description: deliver is now async, but flush calls it without await. The returned coroutine object is always truthy, so every digest is treated as delivered. Lines are deleted from the queue even when delivery fails, `failed` is always empty, and nothing is actually sent (the coroutine never runs, producing a 'never awaited' warning).
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

suppressed_findings.title: Mutating the dict during iteration once flush awaits
suppressed_findings.description: Once deliver is awaited, other tasks can call add() while flush is suspended. add() on a defaultdict can insert a new recipient key, and flush deletes keys from self._pending. The loop iterates over sorted(self._pending), which is a snapshot list, so the iteration itself is safe. However, `del self._pending[recipient]` after the await runs when lines is empty. A concurrent add() for that recipient appends to the same list object, which is fine, but if the entry was already removed and re-created it could raise KeyError. The `if not lines` check and the del are not interleaved with an await, so this is mostly safe. The remaining risk is that the snapshot may include recipients that no longer exist, so `self._pending[recipient]` at line 42 could create an empty list through the defaultdict.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Fetch with `self._pending.get(recipient)` and skip if missing or empty.

findings.title: Coroutine from deliver() is not awaited
findings.description: deliver is now async, but flush calls it without await. The result is a coroutine object, which is always truthy, so every digest is treated as delivered. The coroutine is never run, so nothing is sent. Lines are deleted from the queue, data is lost, and `failed` is always empty. Python also emits a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning.
findings.suggestion: Use `if await deliver(channel, message):`.

suppressed_findings.title: Queue mutation across await can drop or corrupt lines
suppressed_findings.description: The code is meant to keep lines queued during the send, but the loop iterates over `sorted(self._pending)`, which is a snapshot. Once the await is added, `add()` may run during the send and append to `lines`; `del lines[:sent]` handles that. However `del self._pending[recipient]` happens only if `lines` is empty. A concurrent flush of the same queue can also resend the same lines or delete them twice. Because `lines` is a reference to the live list, `render(lines)` is evaluated before the await, so this is mostly fine, but overlapping flushes are unsafe.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Snapshot the lines with `lines = list(self._pending[recipient])` and guard flush with an asyncio.Lock. On success, remove the sent prefix from the live list.

findings.title: for_account filters on the removed `user_id` key
findings.description: `records()` now returns records upgraded to the current schema, so `user_id` is stripped and replaced by `account_id`. `record.get("user_id")` is therefore always None and `for_account` yields nothing, whether the data is old or new. `account_timeline` always returns an empty list as a result.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: for_account filters on legacy `user_id` key that records() no longer yields
findings.description: records() now upgrades every record to the current schema, which removes `user_id` and uses `account_id`. `record.get("user_id")` is therefore always None, so for_account never matches anything. As a result account_timeline always returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: for_account filters on legacy `user_id` key that records() has already removed
findings.description: records() now runs every record through upgrade_record, which drops `user_id` and stores it as `account_id`. New records are written with `account_id` only. `record.get("user_id")` is therefore always None, so for_account never matches anything and account_timeline always returns an empty list.
findings.suggestion: Compare `record.get("account_id") == account_id`.

findings.title: decide() treats the list of violations as a pass/fail boolean, inverting approval
findings.description: check() now returns a list of problem strings, which is empty when the report is within policy. `if check(report, rates):` is therefore true exactly when there are violations. Over-limit reports or reports with missing receipts get auto-APPROVED, and compliant reports are sent to NEEDS_REVIEW.
findings.suggestion: Approve only when the list is empty: `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else: report.status = Status.NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: decide() treats the list of violations as a pass flag, so approval is inverted
findings.description: `check` used to return True when the report was within policy. It now returns a list of problem messages, which is empty when the report is compliant. `if check(report, rates):` is therefore true only when violations exist. Reports that break policy (over the limit or missing receipts) are auto-approved, and compliant reports are sent to a manager as NEEDS_REVIEW.
findings.suggestion: Invert the condition: `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else: report.status = Status.NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: decide() treats the list returned by check() as a boolean, inverting approval
findings.description: check() now returns a list of problem messages (empty when the report is within policy). `if check(report, rates):` is true exactly when there are violations, so over-limit or receipt-less reports are auto-APPROVED. Compliant reports get NEEDS_REVIEW instead. The approval decision is inverted on the main path.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not check(report, rates): report.status = Status.APPROVED else NEEDS_REVIEW`.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes removed `attempts=1` kwarg, which is now sent in the JSON body and retries are enabled
findings.description: The client's keyword was renamed from `attempts` to `max_attempts`, but create_ticket was not updated. `attempts=1` now falls into **fields and is sent to the API as a body field. `max_attempts` stays at the default of 3, so the non-idempotent POST /tickets is retried on transport errors or 5xx, which can create duplicate tickets. The vendor may also reject the unknown `attempts` field.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the create_ticket call.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes the renamed `attempts` kwarg, so it becomes a JSON body field and retries are enabled
findings.description: The `request` parameter was renamed from `attempts` to `max_attempts`, and `add_comment` was updated, but `create_ticket` still passes `attempts=1`. It is no longer recognised and falls into `**fields`, so `attempts: 1` is sent in the JSON body to the vendor API (it may be rejected or ignored). `max_attempts` stays at the default of 3, so the non-idempotent POST is retried on transport errors and 5xx responses. A retry after a timeout can create duplicate tickets, which `attempts=1` was meant to prevent.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the create_ticket call.

findings.title: create_ticket still passes renamed `attempts=1`, so it becomes a body field and retries are re-enabled
findings.description: `request` now takes `max_attempts`. The `attempts=1` call in create_ticket was not renamed, so it falls into `**fields` and is sent to the API as a JSON body field `attempts`. `max_attempts` keeps its default of 3. POST /tickets is non-idempotent, so a timeout or 5xx can now be retried and create duplicate tickets. The vendor may also reject or ignore the unexpected `attempts` field.
findings.suggestion: Change `attempts=1` to `max_attempts=1` in the create_ticket call.

findings.title: Sink write failures are recorded as a rejection of the current row
findings.description: The try block wraps both parse_row and self._flush, and the handler catches Exception. If sink.write raises (DB outage, constraint error), the exception is swallowed and logged as a rejection of the row that happened to fill the batch. Because `pending, batch = batch, []` runs before the flush, the whole batch of up to batch_size already-parsed rows is dropped without being written. Nothing is retried and nothing is surfaced as a sink failure. The load continues, and the report shows only one rejected row, so up to 500 rows are lost silently. After repeated failures it raises a misleading TooManyRejected.
findings.suggestion: Only wrap parse_row in the try/except, and perform the batch flush outside it so sink errors propagate. For example: try: tx = parse_row(row) except ValueError as exc: record rejection; continue. Then batch.append(tx) and flush if the batch is full.

suppressed_findings.title: Overly broad except Exception around parsing
suppressed_findings.description: Catching every Exception treats programming errors such as TypeError or KeyError bugs, and a None row, as data rejections. These get hidden in the report instead of failing fast. A DictReader row with a missing column can also yield None values and trigger AttributeError. That is arguably a data problem, but it is indistinguishable from a bug.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch the specific exception type parse_row raises for malformed input (e.g. ValueError or a ParseError).

findings.title: Sink write failures are recorded as a rejection of the current row
findings.description: The try block also wraps self._flush(), so an exception from sink.write (I/O or DB error) is caught by `except Exception`. The whole batch of up to batch_size rows is dropped because `batch` was already reset to []. Only the single row that triggered the flush is reported as rejected, with the sink's error message. The load then continues and returns a report that looks mostly successful. Rows are lost silently and sink outages are treated like bad data.
findings.suggestion: Only wrap parse_row in the try/except, and call self._flush outside it so sink errors propagate. For example: try: tx = parse_row(row) except ValueError/parse error as exc: record rejection; continue; then batch.append(tx) and flush when full.

findings.title: Sink write failures are recorded as a rejection of the current row
findings.description: The try block wraps self._flush as well as parse_row. If the sink raises (DB outage, constraint error), the except clause records it as a rejection of the row that happened to fill the batch. `pending, batch = batch, []` has already emptied the batch, so up to batch_size rows are silently discarded. The load then continues, and the report shows one rejection for a row that was valid. A persistent sink failure can burn through the rejection budget, or if the budget is not exhausted the load finishes as if only a few rows were bad. Real data loss is hidden from the caller.
findings.suggestion: Catch only parse errors around parse_row, and call self._flush outside the try so sink errors propagate. For example: try: tx = parse_row(row) except Exception as exc: record rejection; continue. Then append tx and flush if the batch is full.

findings.title: charge() returns None after retries are exhausted instead of raising GatewayError
findings.description: When the last attempt fails, the code logs and breaks out of the loop, and the function falls off the end and returns None. settle_invoice only catches GatewayError, so it treats the None as a successful charge and executes `charge.id`, raising AttributeError. That AttributeError escapes settle_open_invoices and aborts the whole batch. The invoice is never marked PAYMENT_FAILED and the remaining invoices are not processed.
findings.suggestion: Keep the last exception and re-raise it after the loop, e.g. `raise` inside the `if attempt == attempts:` branch instead of `break`.

suppressed_findings.title: Gateway is invoked with an idempotency_key keyword that RetryingGateway's positional signature must match
suppressed_findings.description: settle_invoice calls charge(..., idempotency_key=...) which works with the wrapper's parameter name. However, the wrapper forwards the key positionally to the underlying gateway, which may name or order its parameters differently, so it can pass it to the wrong parameter.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Forward the key by keyword: self._gateway.charge(customer_id, amount_cents, currency, idempotency_key=idempotency_key).

findings.title: charge() returns None after exhausting retries instead of raising
findings.description: When the last attempt fails, the loop breaks and the method falls off the end, so it returns None. It does not re-raise the GatewayError. settle_invoice then takes the success path: it sets the status to PAID and reads `charge.id`, which raises AttributeError on None. This happens on any persistent gateway failure, so the invoice is not marked PAYMENT_FAILED. The AttributeError escapes settle_invoice and aborts the whole settle_open_invoices batch. The invoice is left in an inconsistent state: status already set to PAID, but charge_id never assigned.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise the last GatewayError after the final attempt. Replace the `break` with `raise`, or save the exception and raise it after the loop.

findings.title: charge() returns None after retries are exhausted instead of raising
findings.description: When the final attempt fails, the loop breaks and the method falls off the end, implicitly returning None. The last GatewayError is swallowed. In settle_invoice the call then succeeds without raising, so the `except GatewayError` branch never runs, and `charge.id` raises AttributeError on None. The settlement job crashes on the first invoice whose charge fails all retries, and the remaining invoices are never processed. The invoice is never marked PAYMENT_FAILED.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise the last GatewayError after the final attempt (e.g. `raise` instead of `break`, or store `last_exc` and raise it after the loop).

findings.title: finally block overwrites the retry backoff next_run
findings.description: The `finally` clause runs after both the success and failure paths, so `job.next_run = now + job.interval` always replaces the value set in the except branch (`now + self._retry_delay(job)`). The new retry/backoff feature therefore has no effect: failed jobs are rescheduled a full interval later, exactly as before. `retry_delay` is validated and documented but never used in practice.
findings.suggestion: Set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the `else` branch (success path) and drop the `finally`, so the failure path keeps its backoff-based next_run.

suppressed_findings.title: Unbounded exponent in backoff computation can overflow
suppressed_findings.description: `job.retry_delay * 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1)` grows without bound if `max_failures` is large. A huge multiplier makes timedelta multiplication raise OverflowError before `min` caps it. That exception escapes `_run`'s except block, so the record is never appended and `tick` aborts.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent, for example `min(consecutive_failures - 1, 30)`, or compute the delay iteratively and stop once it reaches `job.interval`.

findings.title: finally block overwrites the retry-delay next_run on failure
findings.description: The `finally` clause runs after both the success and failure paths. On failure, `job.next_run` is set to `now + retry_delay` at line 65, then `finally` immediately overwrites it with `now + job.interval`. The backoff/retry_delay feature therefore never takes effect: failed jobs wait a full interval before retrying, contrary to the Job docstring.
findings.suggestion: Set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the `else` branch (or before the try), and remove the `finally` block so the failure path keeps its retry delay.

suppressed_findings.title: Unbounded exponent in backoff computation
suppressed_findings.description: `job.retry_delay * 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1)` grows without bound if `max_failures` is large. Jobs are disabled at max_failures, but a very large max_failures (or a job whose count is set externally) can make the integer huge and `timedelta * int` raise OverflowError. That exception would escape `_run`'s except block and break the tick.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent, e.g. `2 ** min(job.consecutive_failures - 1, 20)`, or catch OverflowError and fall back to `job.interval`.

findings.title: finally block overwrites the retry-delay next_run on failure
findings.description: The `finally` clause always runs, so on a failure `job.next_run = now + self._retry_delay(job)` (line 65) is immediately replaced by `now + job.interval`. The new backoff/retry_delay feature therefore never takes effect and failed jobs wait a full interval before retrying. The `finally` also runs for BaseException, which would set next_run while the exception propagates.
findings.suggestion: Remove the `finally` and set `job.next_run = now + job.interval` only in the `else` branch (success path), keeping the retry-delay assignment in the `except` branch.

findings.title: Unbounded exponent in backoff can raise OverflowError
findings.description: `job.retry_delay * 2 ** (consecutive_failures - 1)` is computed before capping with `min`. If max_failures is large (the constructor only requires >= 1) and a job keeps failing, the huge multiplier makes timedelta multiplication raise OverflowError. This is raised inside the `except` handler in `_run`, so it escapes `tick` and aborts all remaining due jobs.
findings.suggestion: Cap the exponent, or compare the multiplier against interval/retry_delay before multiplying, e.g. `factor = min(2 ** min(n-1, 30), ...)`.

findings.title: sign_out_everywhere swallows StoreError, so change_password can leave sessions alive
findings.description: When a delete fails with StoreError, the loop logs a warning and continues, then returns a count with no failure signal. change_password calls this right after the password is changed and does not check the result. If the store write fails, the old sessions and their refresh tokens stay valid after a password change. The caller only sees a smaller revoked count.
findings.suggestion: Let StoreError propagate, or collect failures and raise after the loop. change_password should fail loudly if any session could not be revoked.

findings.title: _read_all treats a corrupt or unreadable file as an empty store
findings.description: OSError, ValueError and KeyError all return {}. A transient read error or a malformed file is therefore treated as having no sessions. The next save(), delete() or take_by_refresh() then calls _write_all with that empty dict plus one record, which overwrites the file and silently drops every other user's session. A truncated file or a TypeError from a non-list payload is also handled badly. A missing file is the only case that should map to empty.
findings.suggestion: Return {} only for FileNotFoundError. For other read or parse failures, raise StoreError so callers do not overwrite the file.

suppressed_findings.title: Unlocked reads race with the tmp-file write in FileSessionStore
suppressed_findings.description: get() and all() read the file without holding self._lock. The write goes through a tmp file and os.replace, so a plain read is mostly atomic. The same tmp name is used for every write, though, and _read_all swallows errors into an empty dict. A transient read failure during a concurrent write therefore makes get() return None and authenticate() reject a valid session. It also makes all() return an empty list, so sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired do nothing.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Take self._lock in get() and all(), and have _read_all raise on errors other than a missing file.

suppressed_findings.title: Refresh token is consumed before validation and the new session is issued separately
suppressed_findings.description: take_by_refresh deletes the record before the expiry and active checks, and before _issue saves the new one. If _issue fails (for example with a StoreError on save), the old session is already gone and no new one exists, so the user is logged out. The checks themselves are fine, since expired or inactive tokens should die anyway. The partial-failure window is the real issue.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Make rotation a single store operation, or restore the old record if _issue fails.

findings.title: change_password swallows revocation failures, leaving old sessions alive
findings.description: change_password returns sign_out_everywhere(), which catches StoreError per record, logs a warning and continues. If a delete fails (e.g. the file store cannot write), the old session stays valid and still authenticates with its access and refresh tokens, even though the password was just changed. The caller only receives a smaller count and cannot tell that revocation was incomplete.
findings.suggestion: Do not swallow errors when revoking for a password change. Let StoreError propagate, or raise or return an explicit failure when revoked is less than the number of the user's sessions, so the caller can retry.

findings.title: Read errors are treated as an empty store, then written back and wiping all sessions
findings.description: _read_all returns {} on any OSError, ValueError or KeyError (a transient read failure, a corrupt file, a partially written file). save, delete and take_by_refresh then run read-modify-write on that empty dict and write it back. One failed read therefore silently erases every other live session. Meanwhile get() sees every session as missing, so all users appear logged out. The failure is hidden rather than raised as StoreError.
findings.suggestion: Treat only FileNotFoundError as an empty store. Raise StoreError for other read or parse failures so the mutating methods abort instead of overwriting the file.

suppressed_findings.title: Unlocked reads race with writes and with the shared .tmp file
suppressed_findings.description: FileSessionStore.get and all() call _read_all without taking the lock. A concurrent reader can hit the file during a replace or the Windows replace window. Any OSError or ValueError there is swallowed as an empty store. The reader then sees no sessions, so authenticate raises InvalidSession and a valid user is rejected. The same empty result feeds sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired, which then silently do nothing.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Take self._lock in get() and all(), and make _read_all raise on errors other than a missing file.

suppressed_findings.title: Refresh token consumed before validation checks
suppressed_findings.description: take_by_refresh removes the session before the expiry and active checks. If _users.get raises, or _issue fails with a StoreError on save, the old session is already deleted and the client has no valid tokens. The user is logged out by a transient failure.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Check the user's state and make the failure path safe, or re-save the record if issuing the new session fails.

suppressed_findings.title: MemorySessionStore.get reads without the lock
suppressed_findings.description: get() accesses the dict without the lock used by the other methods. In CPython a single dict.get is atomic, so this is mostly benign, but it is inconsistent with the locking elsewhere in the class.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Acquire self._lock in get().

findings.title: change_password silently leaves sessions alive when revocation fails
findings.description: sign_out_everywhere catches StoreError per record, logs a warning and carries on, so it only returns a smaller count. change_password ignores whether every session was ended, even though its docstring promises that. If the file store fails to write, the old sessions stay valid after a password change (for example a stolen access or refresh token) and the caller is never told. The count returned does not reveal this, since the caller does not know how many sessions existed.
findings.suggestion: Re-raise or aggregate failures from sign_out_everywhere, or have it report failures to the caller, so change_password fails loudly when any session could not be revoked.

findings.title: Corrupt or unreadable session file is treated as empty and then overwritten
findings.description: _read_all catches OSError, ValueError and KeyError and returns {}. A corrupt file, a transient read error, or a record missing a field makes the store look empty. The next save, delete or take_by_refresh then rewrites the file from that empty dict, permanently wiping every other session. A single malformed record also discards all valid ones.
findings.suggestion: Treat only FileNotFoundError as empty. Raise StoreError for other read or parse failures, and skip or quarantine individual bad records instead of dropping the whole file.

suppressed_findings.title: Unlocked reads race with non-atomic temp-file writes
suppressed_findings.description: FileSessionStore.get and all read the file without taking self._lock. The writer uses a fixed temp name and os.replace, so reads never see a partial file. However, sign_out_everywhere and purge_expired iterate over a snapshot from all() and delete records afterwards, and a concurrent refresh can have already rotated the record, so the delete targets a stale hash. Separately, MemorySessionStore.get reads the dict without the lock.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Take the lock in get and all, or document and accept the snapshot semantics. Prefer a store-level delete_by_user operation that runs atomically under the lock.

suppressed_findings.title: Refresh token consumed before validation; failed refresh destroys the session
suppressed_findings.description: take_by_refresh removes the record before the expiry and active checks. If the refresh token is expired, or the user is deactivated, the session is already deleted. More importantly, if _issue then fails with a StoreError on save, the old session is gone and no new one exists, so the user is logged out with no way to retry.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Handle failure of _issue by restoring the old record, or perform the take and the save in a single store transaction.

suppressed_findings.title: purge_expired aborts on the first store error and stays quadratic on the file store
suppressed_findings.description: purge_expired calls delete in a loop without handling StoreError. One failed write aborts the purge after some deletions, and the caller gets an exception instead of a count. On FileSessionStore each delete re-reads and rewrites the whole file, so purging N sessions costs O(N²) I/O.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Add a bulk delete to the store, or catch StoreError per record as sign_out_everywhere does.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes the score of every term not in the title
findings.description: `frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Any body term that is not in the title gets a score of 0.0 instead of its frequency. When the title is empty (the default), every keyword scores 0.0 and ranking collapses to alphabetical order. In `suggest_tags`, 0.0 is below MIN_SCORE, so articles get no suggestions except for title terms.
findings.suggestion: Write `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes the score of every term not in the title
findings.description: `scores[term] = frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Every term absent from the title gets a score of 0.0, so body frequency is discarded. Ranking then only favours title terms, and the rest are ordered alphabetically. With no title (the default), every score is 0.0, so extract_keywords returns alphabetically first terms with score 0.0, which breaks existing callers. suggest_tags then filters them all out with MIN_SCORE.
findings.suggestion: Add the bonus conditionally: `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: Conditional expression precedence zeroes the score of every term not in the title
findings.description: `frequency + title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0` parses as `(frequency + title_bonus) if term in title_terms else 0.0`. Terms absent from the title get score 0.0 instead of their frequency. With no title (the default), every score is 0.0, so extract_keywords returns alphabetically ordered terms with score 0. In suggest_tags nothing reaches MIN_SCORE, so no tags are suggested unless the term appears in the title.
findings.suggestion: Use `scores[term] = frequency + (title_bonus if term in title_terms else 0.0)`.

findings.title: updated_at is not advanced on a denied check, so refill is double-counted
findings.description: On the deny path (line 71) bucket.tokens has already been increased by elapsed * rate, but updated_at is left at the old value. The next check recomputes elapsed from the stale timestamp and adds the same interval's refill again. A client that keeps retrying while denied therefore gets refilled faster than the configured rate. For example, with rate 1/s and cost 5, retrying every second will be allowed well before 5 real seconds have passed. The limiter lets through more traffic than configured, and the retry_after value it returns is too optimistic.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now immediately after refilling the tokens (line 69), before the allow/deny branch.

findings.title: Token bucket loses refill progress on denied requests
findings.description: On a denied request, `bucket.tokens` is updated with the refill but `bucket.updated_at` is not. The next check computes elapsed from the old timestamp and adds the same elapsed time to the already-refilled tokens, so the refill is counted twice. This over-grants tokens, and the retry_after hint is also wrong. For example, a client retrying repeatedly while denied gets tokens credited multiple times for the same interval, so the effective rate exceeds the configured limit.
findings.suggestion: Set `bucket.updated_at = now` right after refilling tokens, before the allow/deny check.

findings.title: Bucket updated_at not advanced on denied requests, but refill uses stale timestamp inconsistently
findings.description: On a denied check, tokens are refilled and stored (line 69) but updated_at is not advanced (line 73 is only reached on success). The next call computes elapsed from the old updated_at and adds refill for that whole span again on top of the already-refilled tokens. Refill is therefore double-counted, so clients get more tokens than the configured rate allows. For example, with rate 1/s, tokens 0 and a cost-5 request, polling every second makes tokens grow 1, 3, 6 instead of 1, 2, 3, and the request succeeds early. The Retry-After value is also wrong.
findings.suggestion: Set bucket.updated_at = now right after updating bucket.tokens (before the allow/deny branch), so the denial path does not re-add the same elapsed time.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), but the lookup builds (account_id, prior, metric). It never matches, so previous_total is always None and the change column always shows n/a.
findings.suggestion: Use usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: Daily quantity accumulator not reset between groups
findings.description: After yielding a DailyTotal when the key changes, `quantity` is not reset to 0. The next group starts from the previous group's total, so all later days, accounts and metrics are inflated by earlier totals.
findings.suggestion: Set quantity = 0 after yielding when the key changes, before adding the current event's quantity.

suppressed_findings.title: Zero previous total treated as missing
suppressed_findings.description: `if not self.previous_total` is true for 0 as well as None, which is conflated with no previous data. The result is the same n/a, but the intent is mixed up; the zero-baseline case is handled only by accident. The check is imprecise rather than harmful.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Check `is None` and `== 0` explicitly if different handling is intended.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), and line 66 unpacks it that way. The lookup on line 69 builds (account_id, prior, metric), so it never matches. previous is always None, so previous_total is always empty and change is always n/a. The month-over-month feature is broken.
findings.suggestion: Use usage.get((account_id, metric, prior)).

findings.title: Daily quantity accumulator never reset between groups
findings.description: After a group is yielded on a key change, `quantity` is not reset to 0. The next group starts from the previous group's total, so every daily total after the first includes all earlier quantities. This inflates daily, monthly, peak and average values.
findings.suggestion: Set quantity = 0 after yielding when the key changes, before adding the current event's quantity.

suppressed_findings.title: Sort key may break grouping by UTC day
suppressed_findings.description: The docstring promises UTC days, but the code calls event.timestamp.date() without converting to UTC. Timestamps with non-UTC offsets are bucketed by their local date. Sorting naive and aware datetimes together would also raise TypeError.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Normalize with timestamp.astimezone(timezone.utc).date() when the timestamp is timezone-aware.

findings.title: Daily quantity accumulator is never reset between groups
findings.description: After yielding a DailyTotal when the key changes, `quantity` is not reset to 0. The next group starts with the previous group's quantity, so each later day/metric/account total is inflated by all earlier totals. Monthly totals, peaks, averages and change percentages are therefore wrong whenever there is more than one group.
findings.suggestion: Set `quantity = 0` right after the yield, before `current = key`.

findings.title: Previous-month lookup uses wrong key order
findings.description: UsageKey is (account_id, metric, month), but the lookup builds (account_id, prior, metric). It never matches, so `previous` is always None. previous_total is always empty and change is always 'n/a'.
findings.suggestion: Use `usage.get((account_id, metric, prior))`.

suppressed_findings.title: Zero previous total treated the same as missing
suppressed_findings.description: `if not self.previous_total` returns None for a previous total of 0 as well as None. Both show 'n/a', which is arguably intended for zero (division by zero), but the check also conflates the two cases. The zero case is at least guarded against division by zero.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Check `is None` and `== 0` explicitly if distinct output is wanted.

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared `{}`. `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it, so the first call without metadata stores that key's guessed content type in the shared default dict. Every later `put` without metadata then reuses it and writes the wrong content type, for example `text/csv` for a PDF. A caller-supplied dict is also mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and build a copy: `meta = dict(metadata or {}); meta.setdefault(...)`.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob leaves inconsistent state on failure
findings.description: The metadata file is replaced before the blob is written. If the blob write fails (disk full, I/O error), the old blob stays on disk with the new metadata, or an orphan metadata file is left for a key that has no blob. An overwrite also exposes a window where the old blob is paired with the new metadata.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata. Alternatively, clean up the metadata file or roll it back if the blob write fails.

suppressed_findings.title: head() can fail on a corrupt or partial metadata file
suppressed_findings.description: `json.loads` on the metadata file is unguarded, so malformed content raises a raw `JSONDecodeError` from `head`. If the file is valid JSON but not a dict, `.pop` raises `AttributeError`. The metadata file can also be deleted between `is_file()` and `read_text()`, which raises `FileNotFoundError`.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch `FileNotFoundError`, `ValueError` and a non-dict result, and fall back to empty metadata.

findings.title: Mutable default `metadata` dict is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared `{}`, and `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it. The first call that omits metadata stores the guessed content type in the shared default dict. Every later call without metadata then reuses that type, regardless of its key's extension. Example: put('a.png', ...) followed by put('b.csv', ...) stores image/png for b.csv. Callers who pass their own dict also get it mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and build a fresh copy: `metadata = dict(metadata or {})` before calling setdefault.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob; failed blob write leaves inconsistent state
findings.description: The meta file is atomically replaced before the blob is written. If the blob write fails (disk full, I/O error), the old blob stays with the new metadata, and a first-time put leaves orphan metadata. Metadata for an existing key is therefore changed even though the put failed. The temp files are also not cleaned up on failure.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata. Alternatively, clean up and roll back on failure.

suppressed_findings.title: head() can crash on corrupt or non-dict metadata, and races with delete
suppressed_findings.description: `json.loads` of a corrupt or truncated meta file raises JSONDecodeError, which is not translated to a store error. The is_file check followed by the read is a TOCTOU, so a concurrent delete raises FileNotFoundError. A non-dict JSON value would make `.pop` raise AttributeError.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Wrap the read and parse in try/except (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) and fall back to {} or raise a clear store error.

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated by setdefault
findings.description: `metadata` defaults to a shared `{}`. `put` calls `metadata.setdefault("content-type", ...)` on it, so the first call without metadata stores a guessed content-type in the shared default. Every later call without metadata then reuses that type, so a `.png` put after a `.txt` put is stored as text/plain. A caller-supplied dict is also mutated.
findings.suggestion: Use `metadata: dict[str, str] | None = None` and build a new dict inside: `meta = {**(metadata or {})}`, then `meta.setdefault(...)`.

findings.title: Metadata written before blob, leaving inconsistent state on failure
findings.description: The metadata file is replaced before the blob is written. If writing the blob fails (disk full, I/O error), the old blob stays but carries the new metadata. For a new key, an orphan meta file is left behind, and the failed `.tmp` file is never cleaned up. A concurrent `head` can also see new metadata with old data.
findings.suggestion: Write the blob first, then the metadata, and clean up temp files on failure.

suppressed_findings.title: Corrupt or unreadable metadata file crashes head
suppressed_findings.description: `json.loads` on the meta file is unguarded. A truncated or corrupt file raises JSONDecodeError out of `head`. The `is_file()` check followed by a read also races with `delete`, which can raise FileNotFoundError instead of BlobNotFound.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch JSONDecodeError and FileNotFoundError and fall back to empty metadata.

findings.title: Linear membership test on a list inside the scan loop
findings.description: `active_skus` is a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` scans the whole list for every scan. The cost is O(scans × active SKUs), which becomes very slow for a large catalog and many scans, such as a full warehouse stocktake.
findings.suggestion: Build a set: `active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Linear list membership test inside scan loop gives quadratic cost
findings.description: `active_skus` is built as a list, so `scan.sku not in active_skus` scans the list for every scan. With a large catalog and many scans (a typical stocktake) this is O(scans × skus) and will be slow.
findings.suggestion: Build a set: `active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Membership test against a list makes unknown_locations quadratic
findings.description: active_skus is built as a list, and `scan.sku not in active_skus` does a linear scan for every scan. With a large catalog and many scans, the cost is O(scans × skus), which can make reconciliation very slow on real stocktakes.
findings.suggestion: Build active_skus as a set: `active_skus = {item.sku for item in catalog.active()}`.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed; holidays reloaded on every is_business_day call
findings.description: The `_holidays_by_year` cache was dropped, so `holidays()` now calls `self._source.holidays(...)` on every invocation. `is_business_day` calls it for each day examined, and `add_business_days`, `roll_forward` and `business_days_between` loop day by day. With `JsonHolidaySource`, each call re-reads and re-parses the entire JSON file from disk. SLA computation over many tickets now does thousands of file reads and parses, which is a large slowdown.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-instance cache keyed by year (the region is fixed per calendar), e.g. `self._holidays_by_year: dict[int, frozenset[date]]`.

suppressed_findings.title: overdue_by_region returns every configured region, including those with no overdue tickets
suppressed_findings.description: The return value is built from `self._calendars.codes`, so regions with no overdue tickets map to empty lists. Meanwhile `self.overdue(...)` raises KeyError for a ticket whose region is not configured, so the result is never keyed by anything beyond the configured codes.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Return only regions that have overdue tickets (`dict(grouped)`), or document that every configured region is present.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed; holidays re-read on every is_business_day call
findings.description: The `_holidays_by_year` cache was dropped, so `holidays()` now calls `self._source.holidays(...)` on every invocation. `JsonHolidaySource.holidays` reads and parses the entire JSON file each time. `is_business_day` is called once per day in `add_business_days`, `roll_forward` and `business_days_between`, so each SLA computation does many file reads and JSON parses. `overdue()` multiplies that by the number of tickets, which makes large batches very slow.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-year cache inside BusinessCalendar (keyed by year, since each calendar is bound to one region). Alternatively, cache the parsed file in JsonHolidaySource.

suppressed_findings.title: overdue_by_region silently drops overdue tickets for regions not in codes
suppressed_findings.description: The returned dict is built only from `self._calendars.codes`. `overdue()` raises KeyError for an unconfigured region before this point, so that case is not silent. However, the result is keyed by configured codes only, which is fine. The real problem is that a single ticket with an unknown region makes `for_region` raise from `due_date`, which aborts the whole `overdue()` run and loses all other tickets.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch the error per ticket and report or skip bad tickets, or validate the region up front, so one bad ticket does not abort the whole batch.

findings.title: Per-year holiday cache removed; holidays re-read on every is_business_day call
findings.description: The `_holidays_by_year` cache was dropped, so `holidays()` now calls the source on every invocation. `JsonHolidaySource.holidays` reads and parses the whole JSON file each time. `is_business_day` calls `holidays()` per day, so `add_business_days`, `roll_forward` and `business_days_between` do a file read and JSON parse for every day they step, and `overdue` multiplies that by every ticket. Large ticket lists become extremely slow.
findings.suggestion: Restore a per-year cache of frozensets in BusinessCalendar, keyed by year (the calendar is already per-region). Optionally also cache the parsed JSON in JsonHolidaySource.

suppressed_findings.title: overdue_by_region drops tickets whose region is not configured
suppressed_findings.description: The result is built only from `self._calendars.codes`. However, `overdue()` calls `for_region`, which raises KeyError for an unconfigured region, so the failure surfaces earlier. A single ticket with an unknown region aborts the whole overdue computation instead of being reported or skipped. One bad ticket therefore hides all other overdue tickets.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Handle unknown regions per ticket (skip and log, or collect them separately) so that one bad ticket does not abort the report.

suppressed_findings.title: Render or other send errors abort the whole campaign with no report
suppressed_findings.description: Only RecipientRefused is caught. A template KeyError or IndexError from body_template.format (line 57) in render, or any other mailer error such as a connection failure, propagates out of send_campaign. The loop stops midway and the caller gets no CampaignReport. Some recipients have already been mailed, but nothing records which ones. Re-running the campaign then sends duplicates to those recipients.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch rendering and transport errors per subscriber, record them in the report (for example a `failed` dict), and continue. Or have the report survive the exception so a retry can skip addresses already sent.

suppressed_findings.title: A non-RecipientRefused error aborts the whole send and discards the report
suppressed_findings.description: send_campaign only catches RecipientRefused. Any other mailer failure (connection error, timeout, SMTP server disconnect) or a render error such as a KeyError/IndexError from body_template.format propagates out of the loop. The caller then gets no CampaignReport, so it cannot tell who was already sent the campaign. A retry would re-send to everyone who succeeded, because there is no record of them.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Catch other exceptions per recipient and record them (e.g. a `failed` dict), or attach the partial report to the exception, so the caller can resume without duplicate sends.

suppressed_findings.title: Dedup marks address as seen only after eligibility checks, so later duplicate can slip through
suppressed_findings.description: In eligible(), an address is added to `seen` only after the confirmed/unsubscribed/list checks pass. Because the dedup key is the lowercased, stripped email, an ineligible record does not block a later record for the same address. Records for the same address with different state therefore make delivery depend on input order, which is a policy question rather than a clear bug. The more concrete issue is in send_campaign, where `report.sent` and `report.refused` use the raw `subscriber.email` rather than the normalized address, so reports can contain case or whitespace variants of the same address.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use a normalized address consistently as the key for dedup, sending and reporting.

findings.title: A single non-refusal send error aborts the whole campaign and the report is lost
findings.description: Only RecipientRefused is caught inside the loop. Any other mailer failure (connection error, timeout, SMTP server error) propagates out of send_campaign. The loop stops partway, so the remaining subscribers are never mailed, and the report of who was already sent is discarded because it is never returned. A retry of the campaign would then re-send to the subscribers who already received it, since no record of them survives.
findings.suggestion: Handle other exceptions per recipient and record them in the report, for example a `failed` dict, or attach the partial report to the raised exception so callers can resume without duplicates.

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The old summarize() loaded each distinct sensor's calibration once and reused it. The new code calls calibrated() for every reading, and that calls source.load(), which runs a SQL query each time. For a batch with N readings from a few sensors this becomes N queries instead of a handful.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id in summarize(), for example in a dict, and pass the cached Calibration to calibrated().

suppressed_findings.title: Inspect reason is misleading when the zone was not rejected
suppressed_findings.description: The inspect branch always reports "N readings out of range". When summary.mean is None only because the zone has no readings, rejected is 0, so the reason reads "0 readings out of range". That does not explain why the zone needs inspection.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Build the reason from the actual cause: no valid readings, or the rejected share above the threshold.

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The old summarize() fetched each distinct sensor's calibration once and cached it in a dict. The new code calls calibrated() for every reading, and calibrated() calls source.load(), so a batch with N readings from a few sensors now runs N SQL queries instead of one per sensor. With large batches this becomes an N+1 query pattern.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within summarize(), for example with a local dict, and pass the cached Calibration into the per-reading logic.

suppressed_findings.title: Misleading 'inspect' reason when the zone was rejected for another cause
suppressed_findings.description: The reason always reads '{rejected} readings out of range'. When the zone has too high a rejected share, it also reports the raw rejected count without the total. The message is not wrong, but a zone with mean None and rejected 0 cannot occur, so this is minor. The message does not say that the zone was flagged because the rejected share exceeded the threshold.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Include the rejected share or total count in the message, e.g. f"{summary.rejected}/{summary.count + summary.rejected} readings out of range".

findings.title: Calibration loaded from the database once per reading instead of once per sensor
findings.description: The old summarize() loaded each distinct sensor's calibration once and reused it. The new code calls source.load() through calibrated() for every reading, so a batch of N readings from S sensors now issues N SQL queries instead of S. With SqlCalibrationSource each load is a DB query, so large batches become much slower.
findings.suggestion: Cache calibrations per sensor_id within summarize(), e.g. a local dict, or have calibrated() accept a pre-loaded Calibration.

suppressed_findings.title: Inspect reason is misleading when the mean is None or when no readings were rejected
suppressed_findings.description: The 'inspect' reason always reads '{rejected} readings out of range'. The branch is reachable only when mean is None or the rejected share is above the limit, so the reason is accurate in those cases. However, a zone whose summary has count=0 and rejected=0 (e.g. built by hand) gives '0 readings out of range', which is misleading.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Build the reason from the actual condition, e.g. 'no valid readings' versus 'X of Y readings out of range'.

findings.title: Every can_bid call re-reads and parses the whole day's log file
findings.description: can_bid calls spend(), which calls log.for_day(). That opens and JSON-parses the entire day file, and the file grows with each impression. eligible() does this once per campaign for every bid request, so the hot path is O(campaigns * impressions_today) disk I/O per request. The previous in-memory counter was O(1).
findings.suggestion: Cache per-day spend in memory, loading it from the log once and updating it on record/refund, or keep a per-campaign index.

suppressed_findings.title: Invalid marker is written to the day file derived from the impression's served_at, but for_day reads only the requested day's file
suppressed_findings.description: mark_invalid writes to the file for impression.served_at.date(), and for_day builds the invalid set only from that same day's file. This works only if the caller passes the original Impression. The marker also depends on served_at being in the same timezone as the day used in append. That is fragile but consistent, so the main risk is that an invalid record has no 'campaign' key and any other reader of the log that indexes record['campaign'] will raise a KeyError.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Include the campaign id in the invalid record, and make every reader skip records with kind == 'invalid'.

findings.title: Every bid check re-reads and parses the whole day's log file
findings.description: can_bid calls self.spend, which calls log.for_day. That opens and JSON-parses the entire day file for the campaign. eligible() does this for every campaign on every bid request, so each request costs O(campaigns x file size), and the cost grows through the day as the file grows. The removed in-memory counters made this O(1).
findings.suggestion: Keep cached per-campaign hourly spend in memory, rebuilt from the log on startup and updated in record/refund.

suppressed_findings.title: Invalid markers are written to the file of the served day, but the refund day may differ
suppressed_findings.description: mark_invalid writes the invalid record into the file for impression.served_at.date(), and for_day builds its invalid set only from that day's file. This works only if the impression passed to refund() carries the original served_at. Correctness depends on the caller preserving that timestamp. If the impression was re-created with a different timestamp, the marker lands in the wrong file and the refund is silently ignored, so the campaign stays overcharged.
