suppressed_findings.suggestion: Validate that the impression was actually appended (or look up its original served_at by id) before writing the marker. Alternatively, store invalid markers in a day-independent file.

findings.title: Whole day file re-read and parsed on every bid check
findings.description: can_bid now calls spend(), which opens and JSON-parses the whole day's log file for each campaign on every bid request. eligible() does this for every campaign, so a bid request costs O(campaigns x log size). The log grows through the day, so latency on the hot bidding path increases steadily, and reads are not cached.
findings.suggestion: Keep an in-memory per-day, per-campaign hourly aggregate, loaded from the log once at startup and updated on record/refund.

suppressed_findings.title: Invalid markers written to the file of the served day, which can differ from the day read
suppressed_findings.description: mark_invalid appends the marker to the file for impression.served_at.date(), and for_day only looks for markers in the same day file. This works if served_at is the same value that append used. But append and for_day bucket by served_at.date() in the datetime's own timezone, while pacing buckets by hour using the same naive/aware value. If a refund arrives with an impression whose served_at differs (for example, reconstructed in another timezone), the marker lands in a different day file and the original impression keeps counting against the budget.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Look up the original record's day or normalise served_at to a single timezone (e.g. UTC) in append, mark_invalid and for_day.

findings.title: Per-key exists/get calls replace the single batched get_many lookup
findings.description: The old code made one `catalog.get_many(locale, wanted)` call. The new loop calls `catalog.exists` and then `catalog.get` for every key and every locale in the chain. That is up to 2 * keys * chain-length catalog calls per bundle. If the catalog is backed by a DB or remote store, this becomes an N+1 query pattern on every page render.
findings.suggestion: Fetch with `get_many` once per locale in the chain, only for the keys still unresolved, and merge the results.

findings.title: Per-key exists/get calls replace single batched get_many
findings.description: The old code fetched all keys with one catalog.get_many call. The new code makes up to two catalog calls (exists, then get) per key per candidate locale. If the catalog is backed by a DB, file or network, this becomes an N+1 pattern, with up to 2*N*len(chain) calls per page bundle.
findings.suggestion: Use catalog.get_many(candidate, remaining_keys) once per locale in the chain, and only look up keys that are still unresolved.

findings.title: Per-key catalog lookups replace the batched get_many call
findings.description: The previous code fetched all keys with a single catalog.get_many(locale, wanted). The new code calls catalog.exists and then catalog.get for every key in every locale of the chain, which is up to 2 calls per key per locale. If the catalog is backed by a DB or file, this is an N+1 pattern and doubles the lookups on hits.
findings.suggestion: Use catalog.get_many per locale on the remaining unresolved keys, walking down the chain.

suppressed_findings.title: fallback_keys compares source against raw requested locale, not the normalised one
suppressed_findings.description: Bundle.locale is set to chain[0], the normalised tag. If a caller passes e.g. 'pt_br' or 'pt-br', the bundle locale becomes 'pt-BR', so this works. But Bundle can also be constructed directly, and more importantly missing_report groups by the normalised locale. The comparison itself is consistent for build_bundle output; the real problem is that the Bundle.locale changes from the requested value to a normalised one, which breaks callers that look up bundles by the original string. The original code kept locale=locale.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Keep the caller's locale in Bundle.locale, or document and update callers to use the normalised tag.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with reader check instead of owner check
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. All other mutating handlers (edit, share, unshare) use _require_owner. A shared reader can destroy data they should only be able to view, and the owner loses the entry.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry; readers should use leave_entry instead.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with reader check instead of owner check
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. Every other mutating handler (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner. A read-only collaborator can therefore destroy the owner's data.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry.

findings.title: delete_entry authorizes with _require_reader instead of _require_owner
findings.description: delete_entry calls _require_reader, so any user the entry is shared with can permanently delete the owner's journal entry. Every other destructive or mutating handler (edit, share, unshare) uses _require_owner. A reader who was only meant to view the entry can destroy it, which is data loss.
findings.suggestion: Use _require_owner(entry, user) in delete_entry.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: Invite codes are bearer credentials that grant workspace membership. They are generated with `random.choices`, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed, so an attacker who sees a few codes could predict others and join workspaces uninvited.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`, or `secrets.token_urlsafe`.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: `accept` rejects revoked links and exhausted links but never checks `now >= link.expires_at`. An expired link can still be used to join the workspace, which defeats the TTL. `is_active` already encodes the full rule but is not used here.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

suppressed_findings.title: Check-then-act on link usage is not atomic
suppressed_findings.description: The `uses >= max_uses` check, `directory.add`, and `link.uses += 1` are separate steps with no lock. Concurrent accepts of a single-use link can all pass the check and all join, exceeding `max_uses`.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Guard accept (check, add, increment) with a lock, or use an atomic increment-and-check.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: The invite code is the only secret that grants workspace membership, but it is generated with `random.choices`, which uses the Mersenne Twister. Its output is predictable once enough outputs are observed, so an attacker who sees a few codes could predict others and join workspaces.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: `accept` rejects revoked or exhausted links, but never checks `now >= link.expires_at`. An expired link can still be used to join the workspace, so the TTL is not enforced. `is_active(now)` already encodes the full rule and is not used here.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

findings.title: Invite codes generated with non-cryptographic PRNG
findings.description: The invite code is the only secret that grants workspace membership, but `random.choices` uses the Mersenne Twister, which is predictable. An attacker who observes a few codes could recover the generator state and predict codes for other links, joining workspaces uninvited.
findings.suggestion: Use the `secrets` module, e.g. `"".join(secrets.choice(CODE_ALPHABET) for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH))`.

findings.title: accept() does not check link expiry
findings.description: `accept` checks only `revoked` and `uses >= max_uses`, but not `now < expires_at`. Expired links can therefore still be used to join a workspace, so the TTL is never enforced. `is_active(now)` already covers all three conditions.
findings.suggestion: Use `if not link.is_active(now): raise InviteNotUsable(...)`.

findings.title: Check-then-act on uses allows exceeding max_uses
findings.description: `uses` is checked, then `directory.add` is called, and only afterwards is `uses` incremented, with no locking. Concurrent accepts of a single-use link can all pass the check and all join, so `max_uses` is exceeded. The shared dict and counter are also unsynchronised.
findings.suggestion: Guard accept with a lock, or reserve a use (increment) atomically before adding the member and roll back on failure.

findings.title: Comp ticket endpoint lacks role authorization
findings.description: comp_tickets uses only require_login, so any logged-in attendee can issue free tickets (up to 50 per request) to any holder. Other privileged endpoints (cancel_event, attendee_list) use require_role. This allows free tickets and exhausting event capacity.
findings.suggestion: Replace require_login with require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) and use the returned user for issued_by.

findings.title: Comp ticket endpoint lacks role authorization
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any logged-in attendee can issue up to 50 free tickets per request to any holder, repeatedly, until the event is sold out. Other privileged routes (cancel_event, attendee_list) use require_role. Free tickets are a privileged operation.
findings.suggestion: Use require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) (or ADMIN only) and take the user from its result.

findings.title: Complimentary ticket endpoint lacks role authorization
findings.description: comp_tickets only calls require_login, so any logged-in attendee can issue free tickets to any holder, up to 50 per request, and repeat the call until the event is sold out. Other privileged routes (cancel_event, attendee_list) use require_role, so this route is the odd one out.
findings.suggestion: Replace require_login with require_role(request.user, Role.STAFF, Role.ADMIN) and then use the returned user for issued_by.

findings.title: Move checks editor rights only on the target board, not the source board
findings.description: move_card loads the card and verifies the actor is an editor only on `to_board_id`. It never checks the actor's role on the card's current board (card.board_id). An editor of their own board can pass any card id from a private board they cannot access and move it into their board. That reads the card and removes it from the victim board. NotFound vs Forbidden behaviour on the source board is also bypassed.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) for the source board before the target check, and fail with the same NotFound/Forbidden semantics.

suppressed_findings.title: Archived card keeps stale position, colliding on unarchive or later use
suppressed_findings.description: archive_card detaches the card and sets archived=True but leaves card.position unchanged. There is no unarchive here, but any later restore or direct position use would collide with other cards. Minor compared to the other issues.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Reset position on archive, or re-insert on restore.

findings.title: Move checks editor rights only on the target board, not the source board
findings.description: move_card loads the card by id and only calls _require_editor on to_board_id. The actor's role on the card's current board is never checked. A user who is an editor on their own board can pass any card id from a board they cannot see and move it into their board. This takes the card away from the victim's board and exposes its contents. A non-member also gets NotFound or success depending on card id, which leaks which ids exist.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) before touching the card, in addition to the check on the target board.

suppressed_findings.title: Archived card keeps its position and can collide when unarchived or listed
suppressed_findings.description: archive_card calls detach, which shifts the siblings down, but the card keeps its old position. This is harmless while it stays archived. Still, nothing resets or validates the position, so any later restore path would insert a card with a stale position that duplicates a sibling's. detach also runs before archived is set, so it works only by relying on that order.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Reset the position when archiving, or make insert always recompute the position on restore.

findings.title: Move checks editor rights only on the target board, not the source board
findings.description: move_card loads the card and only calls _require_editor on to_board_id. The actor's role on the card's current board is never checked. Any user who is an editor on some board of their own can move another board's card into it, which takes the card (and its content) out of a board they may have no access to, or only viewer access. It also lets them read the card via the returned object.
findings.suggestion: Call self._require_editor(card.board_id, actor_id) for the source board before any mutation, in addition to the target check.

suppressed_findings.title: Archived card keeps a stale position and unarchive/other paths are inconsistent
suppressed_findings.description: archive_card calls detach and then sets archived=True, but leaves card.position unchanged. Archived cards are excluded from cards_in_column, so the stale position isn't compacted afterwards. Meanwhile edit_card and view_card still operate on archived cards without any check, so archived cards remain editable. This is inconsistent with move_card, which rejects archived cards.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Reject or explicitly allow edits on archived cards consistently, and reset position when archiving.

suppressed_findings.title: Moving within the same column: detach then insert miscounts position
suppressed_findings.description: On a move within the same column, detach decrements positions of lower cards, but the card keeps its old position and is excluded from `others` in insert, so it works. However, when moving a card to a different board, detach uses card.board_id before reassigning, which is correct. The stale card.position is passed over; the real issue is that `position > len(others)` clamps but detach-then-insert on the same column with position equal to len(others) is fine. Low risk.

findings.title: Partner domain match uses endswith without a dot boundary, allowing look-alike origins with credentials
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` has no label boundary. With partner domain `shop.example`, an attacker-registered `https://evilshop.example` or `https://notshop.example` passes. The response then echoes that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so the attacker's page can call /v1/balance and /v1/redeem with the member's session cookie and read the responses. Redeeming points on the member's behalf is possible too.
findings.suggestion: Match the exact domain or a true subdomain: `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

suppressed_findings.title: Port in origin not rejected for partner origins, and response echoes non-normalised origin
suppressed_findings.description: `parts.hostname` drops the port and userinfo, so `https://user@shop.example:8443` is treated as the partner host. The original origin string is then echoed back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A browser never sends such an origin, but any non-browser caller can. The exact-origin path compares the full string, so the two paths are inconsistent.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Reject origins that have a port or userinfo (compare `parts.netloc` to `parts.hostname`) unless explicitly allowed.

findings.title: Partner domain suffix match lacks a dot boundary, so attacker-controlled domains are allowed with credentials
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` has no label boundary. With partner domain `shop.example`, an origin such as `https://evilshop.example` or `https://attacker-shop.example` passes. The policy then reflects that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. A hostile site can then read the member's balance and POST redemptions using the member's session cookie.
findings.suggestion: Accept only an exact match or a true subdomain: `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

suppressed_findings.title: Origin with port or userinfo is not validated beyond hostname
suppressed_findings.description: `parts.hostname` drops the port and userinfo. An origin like `https://user@partner.example:8443` or one with an arbitrary port is accepted as a partner origin, and the raw string is reflected back. This is looser than the exact-origin matching and widens the trusted set to any port on the partner host.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Reject origins where `parts.username`, `parts.password` or `parts.port` are set, or compare the netloc to the hostname.

findings.title: Partner domain check uses bare endswith, allowing attacker-controlled lookalike domains
findings.description: `host.endswith(domain)` has no dot boundary. With partner domain `shop.example`, the origin `https://evilshop.example` or `https://attackershop.example` passes. The policy then reflects that origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, so any attacker who registers a domain that merely ends with the partner string can make credentialed cross-origin calls. Those calls can read a member's balance and redeem rewards using the member's session cookie.
findings.suggestion: Require an exact match or a subdomain match: `host == domain or host.endswith('.' + domain)`.

suppressed_findings.title: Port and userinfo in origin not constrained for partner match
suppressed_findings.description: For partner-domain matching, `parts.hostname` drops the port and userinfo. An origin such as `https://user@shop.example:8443` is treated as allowed, and the raw header is then reflected back. The path and query check does not cover these components. Origins with arbitrary ports on a partner host are accepted, which is broader than intended.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Compare `parts.netloc` against the hostname, or reject origins where `parts.port`, `parts.username` or `parts.password` is set.

findings.title: Connection is not released when reserve fails
findings.description: `self._pool.release(conn)` sits after the try/except, so it only runs on success. If an InventoryError is raised, the code rolls back and re-raises without releasing the connection. Any other exception, such as a database error from get, put or commit, skips both the rollback and the release. Every failed reserve (insufficient stock, unknown SKU, duplicate order) leaks a pooled connection, and the pool will eventually be exhausted. A non-Inventory exception also leaves uncommitted partial changes on the connection.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except/finally. Roll back on any exception with a bare `except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise`, and call `self._pool.release(conn)` in a `finally` block.

suppressed_findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines are checked independently against the same free stock
suppressed_findings.description: Each line is checked against the stored row, and the reservation is stored with the lines as given. If the same SKU appears twice, each line checks `free` against the stock after the earlier line's `put`, which is correct only if conn.get returns the updated row. If conn.get returns a copy or a cached snapshot, the second check uses stale data and the order can over-reserve. The stored reservation also keeps the duplicate lines, so cancel will subtract them separately. This is only a risk if the connection does not read its own writes.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking, for example with a Counter.

suppressed_findings.title: cancel has no rollback and does not handle a missing stock row
suppressed_findings.description: If a stock row is missing, `conn.get` returns None and `row["reserved"]` raises TypeError. Earlier puts for the order's other lines are already applied to the connection and are never rolled back. The connection is then released to the pool in that dirty state, so a later user of the connection may commit the partial changes.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Wrap the body in try/except that calls `conn.rollback()` on any exception before re-raising, and handle a missing row explicitly.

findings.title: Connection leaked and not rolled back on failure in reserve()
findings.description: Release is only called on the success path. When an InventoryError is raised, the connection is rolled back and the exception re-raised, so release at line 96 never runs. Any other exception (e.g. a DB error from get/put/commit, or a KeyError) skips both rollback and release. Each failure leaks a pooled connection, and the pool eventually exhausts. Uncommitted partial writes may also remain on a connection that is never reset.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise, together with finally: self._pool.release(conn), as in receive() and cancel().

suppressed_findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines can bypass the stock check
suppressed_findings.description: If lines contain the same SKU twice, each line is checked against the stock row independently. Depending on the connection's read semantics (e.g. a cached or uncommitted view), the second check may not see the first increment. The stored reservation still records both lines. Cancelling then subtracts both, so reserved could go negative or the order could oversubscribe.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking and updating, and store the aggregated lines.

suppressed_findings.title: Check-then-act race on reservation and stock without locking
suppressed_findings.description: The duplicate-reservation check and the stock read-modify-write are not atomic. Two concurrent reserve calls can both read the same free/reserved values and each write back, losing one increment and overselling. Two calls for the same order_id can both pass the duplicate check.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use row locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or a serializable transaction, or an atomic conditional update in the DB layer.

findings.title: Connection never released on error paths in reserve()
findings.description: The release is not in a finally block. When an InventoryError is raised, the code rolls back and re-raises, so line 96 is skipped and the connection leaks. Any other exception (e.g. a DB error) skips both rollback and release, leaving uncommitted writes on a connection that is never returned. Repeated InsufficientStock or UnknownSku failures will exhaust the pool.
findings.suggestion: Use try/except/finally: roll back on any exception (except Exception: conn.rollback(); raise) and call self._pool.release(conn) in finally.

findings.title: Rollback only for InventoryError, not other exceptions
findings.description: Non-InventoryError exceptions (e.g. connection or KeyError from malformed rows) occurring after some conn.put calls are not rolled back. The partially updated reservation state may remain pending on the connection, which is then reused by the pool, breaking the all-or-nothing guarantee.
findings.suggestion: Catch Exception (or use BaseException) for rollback and re-raise.

suppressed_findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in lines bypass stock check or use stale rows
suppressed_findings.description: If the same SKU appears in multiple lines, each iteration re-reads the row via conn.get. If the connection returns a cached/shared dict or the read isn't from pending writes, the second line may overwrite the first reservation, under-reserving. Also, cancel later subtracts both quantities, driving reserved negative.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Aggregate quantities per SKU before checking and updating, or reject duplicate SKUs.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists (duplicate upload), the function returns without removing the incoming temp file. Every duplicate put leaves a full-size `upload-<uuid>` file in `incoming/`, so disk usage grows without bound. The old code wrote nothing in this case.
findings.suggestion: Call `incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True)` before returning in the exists branch, or wrap the post-write steps in try/finally that unlinks the temp file.

findings.title: Failure after write leaves temp file behind
findings.description: The cleanup try/except only covers the write loop. If `_path_for`, `mkdir`, or `os.replace` raises (permissions, disk error), the temp file in `incoming/` is orphaned.
findings.suggestion: Extend the try/except (or use finally) to cover the digest computation, mkdir and os.replace, unlinking the temp file on failure.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists, the function returns early without removing the temporary file in incoming/. Every duplicate upload leaves a full-size orphan file behind, so disk usage grows without bound for repeated puts of the same content.
findings.suggestion: Call incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before returning in the existing-target branch. Wrap the digest, exists and os.replace section in try/finally or try/except that cleans up the temp file on failure.

findings.title: Temp file leaked if mkdir/replace fails
findings.description: The cleanup guard only covers the write loop. If _path_for, mkdir or os.replace raises (permissions, disk error), the temp file stays in incoming/ with no cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Extend the cleanup to cover the finalize steps, or unlink the temp file in a finally block unless the replace succeeded.

findings.title: Temp upload file leaked when blob already exists
findings.description: When the target already exists, the function returns early without removing the temp file in incoming/. Each duplicate upload leaves a full-size orphan file behind, so disk usage grows unboundedly with repeated uploads of the same content.
findings.suggestion: Call incoming.unlink(missing_ok=True) before returning when target.exists(). Also wrap the mkdir/os.replace step in try/except to unlink the temp file on failure.

findings.title: Temp file leaked if mkdir or os.replace fails
findings.description: The cleanup try/except only covers the write loop. If target.parent.mkdir or os.replace raises (permissions, disk error, ENOSPC), the temp file stays in incoming/ forever.
findings.suggestion: Extend the try/except to include the finalize step, or use a finally that unlinks incoming with missing_ok=True.

suppressed_findings.title: Root directory collides with 'incoming' digest prefix namespace and may break rename across filesystems
suppressed_findings.description: Incoming dir is under root, which is fine for same-filesystem rename, but the old mkdir of root is now only implicit. More importantly the blob layout uses two-hex-char directories; 'incoming' does not collide. However no durability: data is not fsynced before os.replace, so a crash can leave a zero-length or truncated blob at the final content-addressed path, which is then treated as existing and never repaired.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Call out.flush() and os.fsync(out.fileno()) before closing, prior to os.replace.

findings.title: Eviction bound counts countries, not entries
findings.description: The loop condition uses len(self._keys_by_country), which is the number of distinct countries. It is not the number of cached entries. The cache therefore only evicts once there are more than max_entries countries, so the number of entries is effectively unbounded. With a few countries and many postal codes, memory grows without limit. The max_entries guarantee is broken. The LRU behaviour that the old lru_cache(maxsize=4096) provided is lost.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

suppressed_findings.title: clear() leaves hit, miss and eviction counters unchanged and is inconsistent with the index
suppressed_findings.description: clear() empties both maps, so those stay consistent. Separately, _store overwrites an expired entry for the same key without removing it from the key set. That is harmless because the set is idempotent. The real problem is in invalidate_country: if _keys_by_country holds a key that eviction or clear removed from _entries, `del self._entries[key]` raises KeyError. Eviction does keep the two maps in sync, so this is only a latent risk.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use self._entries.pop(key, None) in invalidate_country.

suppressed_findings.title: Table replacement and cache invalidation are not atomic
suppressed_findings.description: source.replace_country is called first, then calculator.rates_changed. Between the two calls, a concurrent lookup can miss the cache, load from the new table, or hit a stale entry. A stale entry is served until invalidation. Because replace_country is not under the cache lock, a loader running inside the cache lock can read the table while it is being swapped. The docstring claim that a lookup never stores a superseded rate does not hold for this path.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Perform the replace and the invalidation under the same lock, for example by having the cache expose an operation that runs the replace while holding its lock.

suppressed_findings.title: Loader runs while holding the global cache lock
suppressed_findings.description: The loader runs inside `with self._lock`, so every lookup on any key (including cache hits) blocks while one slow rate-source call runs. If the source is a remote or database-backed one, this serialises all tax calculations and stats calls.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Load outside the lock and use a per-country version or generation counter to discard results superseded by an invalidation.

findings.title: Eviction bound counts countries, not entries
findings.description: The loop condition uses len(self._keys_by_country), which is the number of distinct countries, not the number of cached entries. The cache is therefore effectively unbounded: with a few countries and many postal codes it never evicts, so memory grows without limit and max_entries is not honored. The comparison should use len(self._entries). The current check also fails to give the intended LRU bound when max_entries=1 with many postal codes.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

suppressed_findings.title: clear() does not reset stats, and the invalidation/eviction bookkeeping is inconsistent
suppressed_findings.description: invalidate_country and clear remove entries without incrementing counters, which is fine, but the main defect is in the eviction path: _evict_oldest assumes _keys_by_country and _entries stay in sync. After the bound is fixed to count entries, this stays consistent. As written, clear() keeps hit/miss counters, so hit_ratio after clear mixes pre- and post-clear lookups. Minor, but it can mislead admins.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Document or reset counters in clear(), or leave as is deliberately.

suppressed_findings.title: Loader exception path counts a miss and holds a non-reentrant lock during I/O
suppressed_findings.description: The loader runs while holding a non-reentrant threading.Lock. A slow loader blocks all lookups, including hits for other keys. If the loader ever calls back into the cache, it deadlocks. Misses for unknown jurisdictions raise after _misses was incremented, which is acceptable, but the global serialization of loads is a real throughput hazard.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Load outside the lock and use a per-country generation counter to avoid storing superseded rates.

suppressed_findings.title: Table replaced before cache invalidation leaves a stale window
suppressed_findings.description: source.replace_country runs first, and rates_changed runs afterward. Between the two calls, concurrent lookups can still hit cached old rates. A concurrent miss in that window can also load the new rate and then be dropped. The rate seen by invoices may be stale for a short time. TableRateSource is also mutated without any lock while rate_for reads it from the cache thread.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Do the replace and invalidate under a shared lock, or accept and document the window.

findings.title: Eviction bound counts countries, not entries
findings.description: The loop condition uses len(self._keys_by_country), which is the number of distinct countries, not the number of cached entries. max_entries is therefore never enforced across postal codes within a country. The cache grows without bound, and with many postal codes per country memory is exhausted. Eviction only happens when there are more countries than max_entries. Eviction then pops the oldest entry, which does not reduce the country count unless that country's last key goes.
findings.suggestion: Use `while len(self._entries) > self._max_entries:`.

suppressed_findings.title: Expired entry replaced without removing the old one from the index
suppressed_findings.description: An expired entry is overwritten by _store, and the key set is a set, so duplicates are not an issue. However, expired entries are never purged except by LRU eviction, and the intended size bound is also affected. This is minor compared with the eviction bug.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Delete expired entries on lookup, or purge them in _store.

suppressed_findings.title: clear() leaves stale state; invalidate may KeyError
suppressed_findings.description: invalidate_country does `del self._entries[key]` for every key in the index. If the index and entries ever diverge, this raises KeyError. Divergence is possible because the eviction bookkeeping is unreliable. Using pop would be more robust.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Use `self._entries.pop(key, None)`.

suppressed_findings.title: Table replacement and cache invalidation are not atomic
suppressed_findings.description: source.replace_country is called first, then the cache is invalidated. A concurrent lookup between the two calls can hit a stale cached rate. Worse, a cache miss in that window can load the new rate, which is fine, but stale hits continue until invalidation. The class docstring claims invalidation can never be superseded, yet the source mutation happens outside the cache lock. TableRateSource itself is also not thread-safe.
suppressed_findings.suggestion: Perform the replacement and invalidation together under the cache lock, or invalidate before and after the replacement.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes a one-shot iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` iterates `lines` once to count it. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator. After the count, the `for line in lines` loop at line 54 sees an exhausted file and reads nothing. Every run therefore reports read=0 and writes an empty output file, while progress shows 0/N lines.
findings.suggestion: Do not pre-count a generic iterable. Either materialise it with `lines = list(lines)` (which costs memory), or report progress without a total. If a total is needed, count in a separate pass over a re-openable source, such as the path.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: In the `except LookupTimeout` branch, `return enrich(event, geo)` is missing `await`. `enrich_one` returns a coroutine object, not an `Event`. The retry never runs, and a coroutine ends up in the gather results and is passed to `sink`. `to_json` then fails or emits garbage, with a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning. The documented behaviour (retry once, abort on a second timeout) is not implemented.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)` so the retry actually runs and a second LookupTimeout propagates.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes a one-shot iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` exhausts `lines`. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator. The later `for line in lines` loop then sees no lines. The run reads 0 lines and writes an empty output file, and progress reports 0/N.
findings.suggestion: Do not pre-count a generic iterable. Pass the total separately, or materialize with `lines = list(lines)` (costly for large files). Alternatively, report progress without a total.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: In the `except LookupTimeout` branch, `return enrich(event, geo)` lacks `await`. `enrich` is now async, so `enrich_one` returns a coroutine object. The sink then receives a coroutine instead of an Event, and `to_json` fails or the coroutine is never run. The retry never actually happens. A second timeout cannot abort the run as documented. It also runs outside the try block and semantics are lost.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)` in the retry branch.

findings.title: Counting lines consumes a one-shot iterator, so nothing is processed
findings.description: `total = sum(1 for _ in lines)` iterates `lines` once to count it. The CLI passes an open file object, which is a one-shot iterator. After counting, the `for line in lines` loop at line 54 sees an exhausted file and reads nothing. The output is empty, stats show read=0, and progress shows 0/N. Any generator input behaves the same way.
findings.suggestion: Do not pre-count a single-pass iterable. Either materialise it with `lines = list(lines)` (which costs memory), or rewind the file and count separately in the CLI, or report progress without a total.

findings.title: Retry returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of an Event
findings.description: In the `except LookupTimeout` branch, `return enrich(event, geo)` is missing `await`. `enrich` is now async, so `enrich_one` returns a coroutine object. The sink then receives a coroutine rather than an Event, and `to_json` fails or the output is corrupted. The retry never actually runs, and a 'coroutine was never awaited' warning is emitted. A second timeout can never abort the run, as the docstring promises.
findings.suggestion: Use `return await enrich(event, geo)`, so the retry executes and a second LookupTimeout propagates.
